By contrast, theft or murder carried out in the service of a revolutionary idea may be a mistake, but it is not a crime.

The same applies to madness. Anyone who rejects the fundamental truths commonly accepted by society, while making no effort to produce arguments capable of persuading others of the contrary, must be regarded as insane.
In this sense, every “utopian” comes fairly close to madness, if by “utopia” we mean a revolutionary political project that gives no indication of the means by which it could actually be realized.
A political project is revolutionary rather than utopian only when it takes the existing conditions into account and shows how one can begin from them and arrive at a new order.
Only such a project deserves to be discussed, because only such a project can be verified through revolution.

110) It goes without saying that this “circularity” can be fully achieved only in perfect knowledge. Philosophy must nevertheless strive toward it as far as possible, filling out the fragments of knowledge until they close in on themselves as an unbroken circle.
Here as elsewhere, success will be our only judge.
111) From this point on, I will speak of Phenomenology only as an “introduction to philosophy,” not as a path leading to wisdom. This changes the situation somewhat.
Within the circular system of omniscience, there is one and the same Phenomenology: it serves as the introduction to knowledge and also appears as the third and final part of that same knowledge.

Before omniscience has been reached, however, the themes of Phenomenology and those of the final part of the System do not coincide. One could even say that this very failure to coincide reveals the imperfection of knowledge.
All of this will become clearer later.
112) The author writes the introduction after writing the book and can therefore draw on the results reached in it. But the reader reads the introduction before reading the book itself.
For the reader, then, the introduction is only a “project” or “program,” and it can be judged only after one knows whether that program has actually been carried out.
So I ask once again that my book be judged as a whole, rather than having the claims made in the introduction criticized in isolation.

113) What I mean here is neither the complete absence of philosophy nor the appearance of an entirely new philosophy. I mean only the disappearance and appearance of the philosophy that can count as true at a given historical moment, and which must replace the philosophy that, at that moment, can no longer be regarded as fully true.
114) Plato’s “dogmatics” has not survived, while Kant’s Critiques were never followed by the systematic philosophy they were meant to prepare, apart from his moral philosophy and philosophy of law.

There is no doubt, however, that Plato’s treatise On the Good existed. And in the “Introduction” to the Critique of the Power of Judgment, Kant stresses that his Critique is intended only as preparation for a systematic philosophy and must never be allowed to replace it—as the “neo-Kantians” and many modern historians of philosophy believe it does.
115) Once again we have an example of dialectical transformation.

The thesis is the “arrogance” of the philosopher who has not gone through Phenomenology. This gives rise to its antithesis, the “modesty” of the phenomenologist. Their union will produce the synthesis: the “megalomania” of the phenomenological philosopher.
As we are about to see, both earlier elements survive within this synthesis, but in fundamentally transformed form.
116) This does not mean, of course, that everyone is equally capable of doing philosophy. Here as elsewhere, some people are more gifted than others.
But the difference is quantitative, not qualitative.
117) In principle, it is perfectly possible that the System will be written not by the author of the Phenomenology himself but by one of his readers.
118) The struggle against “authority,” especially the authority of the Catholic Church, is particularly characteristic of seventeenth- and eighteenth-century philosophy.
But this struggle belongs to all non-theological philosophy and is already fully conscious in the Greek Sophists and in Plato’s Socrates.
119) There is no contradiction here with what I said earlier about “social verification.”

The philosopher, as a philosopher, cannot set his own opinions against what the society to which he belongs regards as true—provided that this society is not prerevolutionary, meaning destined to disappear.
But first, he must know why he behaves in this way. Second, he must know who the legitimate representative of that society and State is.
He therefore does not submit to this representative as an individual, but to the society that the representative represents.

At present, the legitimate representative of Soviet society as a whole is unquestionably Comrade Stalin. To the extent that Comrade Stalin acts as the representative of that society, his judgment is therefore binding on the Soviet philosopher.
But the philosopher does not accept this judgment simply because Joseph Vissarionovich has said it. Joseph Vissarionovich’s personal opinion is just as suspect as any opinion whatsoever.

Here again we can appeal to the Christian tradition. The Catholic Church draws the same distinction between the Pope’s personal opinion, which may be questioned, and what he says ex cathedra—that is, in his capacity as the representative of the Church—which is not open to dispute.
The error in that case is simply this: the Pope’s authority is supposedly based on “God,” whereas the authority of the leader of Soviet society is consciously and openly based on that society itself.
And if it can be shown that, for the present, this society is the truest one, then the truth of the “authorities” it recognizes has thereby also been shown and proved.

We thus arrive at a kind of “circular guarantee.” By recognizing a given philosophy, society guarantees its “sociohistorical truth”—that is, it guarantees that this philosophy corresponds to the social realities of the historical period in question.

And the philosophy recognized by society, in turn, guarantees the “sociohistorical truth” of that society by showing that, under the given historical conditions, it is the most fully realized society—or, more precisely, the only society that is actually possible: a stable, postrevolutionary society rather than a prerevolutionary one.

120) Before Copernicus, for example, the Sun’s movement around the Earth was regarded as a “scientifically established fact.” Later, the Earth’s movement around the Sun came to be regarded as another such “definitively” established fact.

In recent years, however, Einstein and his successors have held that there is no “fact” here at all, and that the empirical data can be interpreted from either the Ptolemaic or the Copernican standpoint.

So it is clear that either Ptolemy is right, or Copernicus is right, or Einstein is right. And it is equally clear that what we are dealing with here is not a “fact,” but the same empirical astronomical data interpreted through three different theories.
And yet this certainly looks like the sort of case in which we ought to be dealing with a fact!
121) According to Aristotle, for example, one of the basic anthropological facts is the opposition between master and slave. Bourgeois liberalism and socialism, by contrast, reject this fact.

Yet there is no denying that this fact really did exist in the ancient world, and Aristotle was therefore entitled to use it as the basis for his theories about humanity. The difference between master and slave was just as real as, say, the difference between men and women.
But because this fact no longer exists in the bourgeois and socialist world, it would be completely absurd to appeal to Aristotle and “his” fact when constructing a modern theory of humanity.
Here the theory of humanity has to change because human beings themselves have changed, not merely because our knowledge of them has changed.

(It is in principle possible that, in some extremely distant and extremely “utopian” future, we might have to change our anthropological theories again because of the disappearance of another social fact: the difference between man and woman.)
122) Someone might object that all opinions, whether true or false, are part of the real world insofar as they exist in the consciousness of living individuals.

And this is of course correct. In that sense, every opinion present in a real consciousness is simultaneously part of the real world. There would therefore seem to be no way of separating one opinion from the rest and confronting it with reality.
But when I build an airplane, I confront reality only with what is contained in the airplane’s design.
In other words, we can regard as real not only the entire mass of my opinions taken together, but also one particular part of them.

We must therefore distinguish between the reality of a human being, including all the thoughts actually present in that person’s consciousness at a given moment, and the reality of an individual thought, considered independently of whether it happens to be present in this or that consciousness at the moment.
Only the latter can be regarded as “true.”
123) The “technical world” does not consist only of clothes, houses, roads, cars, and so on—that is, of things actually created by human work.
The “technical world” is the real aspect of the natural world as a whole.
The sea, for example, forms part of the natural world because it exists independently of humanity. But it also belongs to the “technical world” insofar as it serves as a “means of transport.”

To the extent that the sea “supports” the ships sailing across it, the two worlds coincide. But when the sea sinks those ships—which is clearly not part of the human shipbuilder’s plan—there is an actual contradiction between them.
Facts of this kind show that the two worlds are still very far from coinciding completely. Their difference is obvious even to a relatively untrained eye.

In other words, the products of human labor are just as real as the products of nature, but they do not always resemble them. A human being can build a car that replaces a horse very effectively, but cannot make the horse itself, at least not in that form.
We can therefore suppose that complete knowledge of the world will be reached only when the difference between the natural world and the technical world has finally disappeared.

Until that happens, we must always remember that human beings live not only in the natural world but also in the technical world. Knowledge of the conditions of the second is just as important for understanding humanity as knowledge of the conditions of the first.
Hegel only glimpsed this truth. Marx was the first to grasp it clearly.

Corresponding to the “fundamental laws” of the natural world—which of course remain valid in the technical world, since the technical world has become a real part of nature—are the “instruments of production” in the technical world: the real possibilities available for constructing it.
The “technical world” can also be called the “economic world.”
124) At first glance, it may seem that the natural world is not yet fully realized either. New kinds of plants and animals appear on Earth, after all, and new stars light up in the sky.

But what changes here is only the “appearance,” so to speak, of the natural world. Its fundamental laws remain unchanged. Newly appearing animals will live according to the same biological principles as the old ones, and new stars will obey the old “stellar” laws.
In the human world, by contrast, the very foundations of the laws and principles governing existence change.
The fundamental law of the ancient world, for example, was the master-slave relation, which disappeared in the Christian and bourgeois world.
The same is true of this latter world: its fundamental law, the “sacred” principle of private property, has disappeared.
125) Human ideas about humanity can go beyond what has already been realized in human existence.
But such an idea is not truth. It is a project. It concerns not what is, but what ought to be.
For that reason, it goes beyond the boundaries of philosophy.
126) A human being, as a human being, is conditioned by the human—sociopolitical—world to which that person belongs.

An individual living in the USSR, for example, may therefore in fact be a “socialist” human being. Yet we know perfectly well that not all citizens of the Union are anywhere near becoming conscious of themselves as this socialist type of human being.
And what is true of separate individuals can also be true of society, and of the State, as a whole.
127) The Christian, for example, understood the pagan better than the pagan understood himself. Today, we understand the thirteenth-century Catholic much better than he understood himself.
We can therefore say that human beings understand their predecessors better than those predecessors understood themselves.
Only at the end of history will the “sage” achieve complete self-understanding.
Indeed, the further a human being stands from a predecessor, the better—or more completely—that predecessor can be understood.
The pagan and the Catholic will therefore become fully intelligible only to the “communist” human being—that is, to the “sage.”
But we will return to this later.
128) The world can, of course, exist without humanity, whereas humanity cannot exist without the world.
But insofar as human beings actually exist, the world necessarily includes them.
To speak of a world without humanity is therefore to speak not of the world that actually exists, but of a world that could exist—in other words, an abstraction.
129) To know something about an electron, for example, one must in some sense see it. To see it, however, one needs colour. But colour has a real effect on the electron.
So what we see is not the electron as it exists independently of being seen. See Heisenberg.
130) So many different “gods” have been invented that it would be very difficult to give a general definition of what a “god” is.
Still, it seems to me that, strictly speaking, one thing can be said of all gods: they can act on human beings, but human beings cannot act on them.
(It follows from this definition that magic is always, in reality, atheistic, even when it does not recognize itself as such.)
As long as we believed, for example, that the Sun acted on us while we did not act on it, the Sun was “divine.”
But once we were told that “every natural action has an equal reaction” and that “the Sun’s radiation on the Earth is reflected toward Sirius,” the whole natural world lost its divine character.
From this we can understand why the “scientist” who forgets that knowledge of the world results from a real interaction between human consciousness and that world so easily falls into theology.
A reality conceived as “independent” of consciousness always takes on something of a “divine” character, whether it is called “spirit” or “matter.”
(Only the dialectical “materialism” of Hegel and Marx is atheistic—that is, it alone aims at concrete knowledge and refuses to sever the real connection between the world and humanity.)
131) In the strict sense, “knowledge” (epistēmē) is always true knowledge.
But there are also false judgments whose falsity reveals itself “always” and “to everyone,” and these can therefore be called false “knowledge.”
Only knowledge, then, can be true or false. Opinion, as opinion, is neither true nor false. It is merely possible—that is, internally consistent—or impossible, meaning internally contradictory.
Clearly, this requirement that knowledge be “universal” should not be taken literally. It concerns only people who actually understand the discourse that makes up the knowledge in question.
If you understand a piece of knowledge, that is enough for you to know that it is true. By contrast, you can fully understand a possible opinion while still judging it mistaken or doubtful.
Only from the standpoint of knowledge can one know whether a given opinion is correct or mistaken.
132) Opinion and ideology presuppose a lack of self-awareness, and lack of self-awareness is in turn sustained by opinion and ideology.
When a person expresses an opinion or develops an ideology, that person does not know that it is merely an opinion or ideology. On the contrary, they believe it to be truth or knowledge.
